utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-09-92-T, The Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Before we start with the next witness there are a few preliminaries, both from the Chamber and, as I understand, also from the Prosecution. First of all, I would like to raise the matter of sitting times on Tuesday, the 15th of January. The Chamber has not received any complaints from the parties about the suggested sitting times for next Tuesday, and, as a result, the Chamber confirms that it will sit on this day from 7.30 in the morning, until 11.55, with three 75-minute sessions, and 20-minute breaks. Then there's one remaining matter in relation to the upcoming witness. The Chamber would like to give an oral decision. The Chamber will deliver its decision on the addition of three documents to the Prosecution's 65 ter list. On the 10th of December, 2012, the Prosecution filed its fifth motion to add exhibits to its 65 ter exhibit list. The Defence did not file a response. The Prosecution contends that the three documents it seems to have added to the 65 ter exhibit list are relevant and probative to the incident detailed in Schedule F11 of the indictment. The Prosecution seeks to amend its 65 ter exhibit list at this stage as it only recently identified the documents after having questioned another witness in the proceedings. The Chamber considers, as conceded by the Prosecution, that this does not amount to a showing of good cause. The Chamber considers, however, that the documents are, prima facie, probative and relevant to the incident at Schedule F11 of the indictment. The Chamber further notes that the Defence has not contested their addition to the 65 ter exhibit list. The Chamber considers that the Defence has had sufficient time to study the three documents, since the Prosecution filed its motion on the 10th of December 2012 and further notes that, according to the Prosecution, the documents were disclosed to the Defence on the 16th of November of last year. The Chamber find s that the accused will therefore not be unduly prejudiced by their addition. Moreover, the Defence will be able to further address any prejudice it may have suffered from the late addition to the Rule 65 ter list when the documents are used and tendered by the Prosecution. Therefore, and despite the absence of good cause, the Chamber finds it to be in the interests of justice to allow the addition of the documents bearing provisional Rule 65 ter numbers 28603, 28604, and 28605 to the Prosecution's Rule 65 ter exhibit list. And this concludes the Chamber's decision. Having dealt with these matters, I also want to convey on behalf of the Chamber the best wishes for 2013 for everyone in this courtroom, how different the situations may be in which we find ourselves in. Then the Prosecution had one matter to raise, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour, and the Prosecution appreciates the Chamber's well wishes. Your Honour, we have a request with respect to the next witness, Dr. Milan Mandilovic scheduled to commence his testimony tomorrow. Your Honours, he is a surgeon who has worked at the Sarajevo state hospital from May 1992 until the end of the war and currently still works there. The Prosecution has given notice by e-mail that it intends to ask the witness about a number of medical documents additional to the documents already addressed in the witness's statement. The primary evidential value of these documents is the information they provide on their face about the medical condition pertaining to victims of scheduled sniping and shelling incidents. Dr. Mandilovic is able to address the issue of authenticity of these documents. In order to deal with these documents in a more efficient way, the Prosecution seeks to employ the mechanism of a chart in the same way we have used this device in the past. As we have in the past, we would not tender the chart or the underlying documents until the Defence has had a full opportunity to examine the doctor. I have previously undertaken to seek advanced approval from the Chamber prior to using this mechanism and do so now, believing that it is an appropriate and efficient way to proceed with respect to these particular documents. I discussed the matter with Mr. Stojanovic prior to the commencement of today's proceedings and he will not be objecting to the use of it as well. So, Your Honour, I ask you to consider that. We have prepared the chart, so if the Chamber at some point today could advise us whether we would be able to use that with this witness, it would be appreciated. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, the Chamber will consider your request and let you know today.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Ms. Hochhauser has a brief matter she wants to inform the Chamber of, but I believe it could be done while the witness is being brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Before I give her an opportunity to do so, the Chamber, from the silence of Mr. Stojanovic, understood that Mr. Groome has well reflected the position of the Defence on the matter of the use of the chart. Can the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Ms. Hochhauser, meanwhile, you have an opportunity to address the Court.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Thank you, and good morning, Your Honours. Your Honours, we will be offering ultimately tendering a public redacted version of this expert report as well as a version under seal. However, during the course of my examination, I will be calling up the under seal version and will state explicitly when the pages are safe to broadcast outside of the courtroom. I have informed Mr. Ivetic of the reasons for this so that he is aware of them. As well, it's that -- in the redacted version due to the way that has to be scanned to be redacted, the pictures are degraded and so the quality of the picture in the under seal version is the one that should be used where there's no protected information on that sheet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So we will look at the redacted version although you will tender the unredacted version as -- in evidence, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: We'll be -- I'm sorry, I'll be tendering both a redact -- sorry. Both an under seal version with redactions as well as -- I'm sorry. An under seal version without the redactions which I will be also showing during the course of the examination because the pages that I'm showing do not have any protected information on them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And those pages can be broadcast to the public so that they can also see the photos on those pictures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Additionally, it's my intention - and I've informed Mr. Ivetic of this well - to tender the report after the Chamber has heard the entire examination of the witness if that -- if that is acceptable to the Chamber so that we can put off any necessary conversation until after the witness has gone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That seems to be a very practical approach. Mr. Ivetic, since you have not jumped up I take it that Ms. Hochhauser has represented your views correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: She has.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And finally, Your Honours, as I'm sure you see in front of you - and I apologise to the witness because he's here in the room - I have handed out hard copies of the report and those are the -- that is the under -- the confidential version that would be under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning, witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. van der Weijden, I take it. Before you give evidence in this Court, the rules require that you make a solemn declaration, the text of which is now handed out to you. May I invite you to stand and to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. van der Weijden. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You will first be examined by Ms. Hochhauser. Ms. Hochhauser is counsel for the Prosecution. Ms. Hochhauser you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Can you please put your name on the record.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Yes. My name is Patrick van der Weijden.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And, Mr. van der Weijden, how are you currently employed?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: I'm currently employed by the Dutch Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And in what capacity? What are your responsibilities in your current position?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: I'm an officer in the Dutch army special forces and in that function I am a team leader of a special force unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Okay. And what is your current rank?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: My current rank is captain.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Now if I could please see 65 ter 28556 on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The speakers are kindly asked to slow down and to pause between questions and answers for the sake of interpretation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And captain, we've been asked by the interpreters to slowdown and pause between question and answer, so I will be making my best effort and if you could do the same. The document that is on the monitor now, 65 ter 28556, is that your curriculum vitae?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And does it accurately reflect your civilian and military education as well as your postings and deployment?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Yes, it does. Although I have left out some military course that I deemed irrelevant for this subject.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Now, in -- in your current job function, are you -- you said you were the team leader of a special forces unit. Does that also involve the teaching and training of other members of the military and of snipers in particular?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: It might. Although my main function is team leader, but I can be called upon to -- as a sniper instructor to instruct other snipers in training.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And the role of sniper instructor, we see it on your CV under selection of military courses that you received that certificate in 2004. Is that something that you have continued to do since then, to instruct and train other people in that skill?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm -- I'd like to tender please 28556 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 28556 becomes Exhibit P669, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Captain, you have testified as an expert witness before this Tribunal in the Prlic et al, Dragomir Milosevic, Perisic, and Karadzic cases. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And did you prepare expert reports for both the Dragomir Milosevic and Karadzic cases?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And was one of those expert reports also used in the Perisic case?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: I believe it was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Were you asked to prepare a report in this cases?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: If we could please place 65 ter 28541 on the monitor and just show the first page although, as I said earlier, this will be a document that I will ultimately ask be placed under seal. The first page can be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Is this the report that you prepared for this case?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: If this report is the same one as the one I've provided in a hard copy, then it will be the same report.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Do you have a hard copy of your report with you?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Yes, I have one here.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And with the Chamber's permission, can the witness maintain that copy during his testimony?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. No problem. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Now can you describe how the report that you prepared for this case relates to the report that you prepared for -- for the earlier cases that we discussed?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: For the -- this report is a mix of some of the incidents of the Milosevic case and the Karadzic case, and, in addition, some of the incidents that were left out earlier have been put in this report as well. So this report is more of an update on the -- both reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Now, if we could turn, please, to the second page in e-court in both the English and B/C/S versions. And in the hard copy, that's the page marked 1 of 84, the page after the cover page.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Now, what we see is an index of the sections contained in the report, and I'm going to begin with asking you some questions about the section that you have entitled at number 1, an introduction to sniping. Now within that section you explain that there are different definitions of the term "sniper" and "sniping" that are in use. And you write on page 2 -- sorry. It would be two of the hard copy, page 3 in e-court in both the English and B/C/S, that: "'Sniper Alley' in Sarajevo is known to the whole world. Since that conflict the word sniper is used to indicate a shooter who shoots at whoever he gets in his sights men, women, children, combatant or non-combatant." And I'd like to ask you in light of what you've written in this section about the various definitions of "sniper" versus "sniper!" And what I've just read out to you, if we can start out by defining the terms that you are going to use in your testimony. So if you could please explain to the Chamber what definition of the words "sniper" and "sniping" you are using when you use those words?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: If I'm using the word "sniper" I refer to the -- to the military sniper that I'm familiar with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could I -- if you look at your screen, you will see that there's another request to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Yes, and I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you, please, you started your answer, that you were using the word sniper referring to the military sniper that you're familiar with. Could you continue from there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The military sniper is an expert marksman that has been trained tactically as well and should be able alone or in a team to approach his targets, to observe his targets, and to eliminate his targets, and then get away unseen from the target area. That's my definition of the military sniper. And the sniper that -- the sniping incidents in general that what most people refer to as a sniping, is, in my view, or are in my view the incidents where people are fired upon by an unseen shooter regardless of what kind of weapon has been used or level of training that the shooter has received. So I don't -- the military sniper might be the sniping of the sniper that people refer to, but not necessarily so.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And when you say regardless of the weapon that is used, are you referring to small arms as well as larger calibre arms or can you clarify that, expand on that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Yes, I will. Small arms would be all handguns up to rifles and machine-guns up to the calibre of 12.7 millimetre, so all the weapons that -- that are have that calibre or below are considered small arms and would be the weapons that I would -- would refer to.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Can you please explain to us the difference between a sharpshooter and a sniper.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: The sharpshooter and a sniper both receive their technical training as for shooting. That training would be the -- more or less the same. The sniper only has advanced training in field tactics so that would enable him to approach target unseen. The sharpshooter receives the same technical training on shooting and is usually -- usually operates within a team and doesn't go out with a small team or by himself.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: For the incidents that you examined, the individual -- excuse me, the individual incidents that you examined in your report. Did you examine whether they would require in your opinion the specialised skill and training of a sharpshooter or a sniper?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Well, some would require a -- at least a shooting background. So a sharpshooter or a sniper might be the one who have -- who would have shot. But -- and a hunter would have an extensive background or some people with a sporting shooting background would also be able to fire some of the shots.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And can you tell us when you -- when you -- excuse me. Can you tell us what factors you would consider in taking into -- into account the best -- excuse me. Can you tell us what factors you would consider in assessing the necessary skill level for a particular shooting?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: They would be the distance, as -- as the main factor, but also the time that the -- that the target would have been visible. But mostly it's distance, wind conditions, and everything that comes with those.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And are there certain distances and certain conditions in which, in your opinion, the use of specialised equipment would also be necessary?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Yes, there are. I believe that above 300 metres then you would already need a very experienced shooter with a standard rifle to be able to fire those shots. So I believe that above 300 metres you would need specialised equipment. The only exception is if machine-guns have been used -- well, machine-guns are sort of standard equipment, so you wouldn't need an accurised [sic] weapon for those.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And can you explain, please, how setting up -- setting up in and continuing to operate from a known location would affect the necessary skill required for the shooter in a particular instance?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Well, I think the longer the shooter is able to stay in a certain position and can operate from that position he will gather more data on the shooting conditions for that location, which would enable him to, over time, make more accurate shots. The downside for the shooter would be that -- that position would be compromised and that would be a bigger threat for him to say in that position.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And can you tell us what measures one could take in order to improve the accuracy of a weapon at longer ranges?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: First of all, would be the -- the position that he would be in. So if he is in a supported position, he can improve his position by putting his weapon in a supported position, so not free offhand shooting but perhaps put his rifle or whatever -- whatever weapon he is using on sandbags. Shooting from a prone position would be more accurate, but if in time it shows that it's very difficult to get better results, you would need optics or a better weapon.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And to -- to define optics?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Optics would be an optical sight with at least three to four times magnification which enables the shooter to -- to spot targets, identify targets, and to engage targets.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Now moving to section 2 of the report which you title "Incident Files," can you briefly explain to the Chamber your methodology in examining each of these incidents?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Yes. I was asked by the OTP. I was given a list of incidents with the general area GPS co-ordinates, a date, and a brief description of the incident. I then asked the -- I asked if I was able to visit the location to get a better feel of the incident, and when I visited the location I worked on -- on the location itself. I would get to the level at which the -- according to the witness statements or the evidence that the bullets had hit the victim, so if it -- the bullet would be at knee height, I would kneel down at knee height and see where the bullet might have come from. And then limits -- eliminate positions that would be tactically unwise or technically [realtime error read in transcript "tactically"] impossible.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And can you tell us specifically what it was you were seeking to determine for -- or seeking to reach an opinion on for each incident?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I before we continue, the transcript reads now "eliminate positions that would be tactically unwise or tactically impossible," but I think you -- I heard you say "technically."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Technically, that's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Both or -- "technically unwise," I don't know what that means. You would say that it would for "technical" reasons unwise to use such a position and not "tactically," because "tactically unwise" seems to be an option as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The -- tactically unwise would be if somebody would be out in the open shooting from that position which would completely compromise his own safety, so that would be tactically unwise and it should be technically impossible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So if there would be a building in the way, that would be technically impossible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So your testimony is now it would be tactically unwise or technically impossible.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Referring back to the question I was asked by the --

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Yes. The question was what was it that you were seeking to reach an opinion about for each incident.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: I was trying to establish where the shooter must have been firing from to be able to -- in the -- in the incident. What kind of weapon he would -- would have used, what distance he would have been at. And if he would be able to identify the target as combatant or non-combatant.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And you referenced witness statements as -- did you accept as fact in witness statements the witnesses' perception of the origin of fire?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Not necessarily so because I believe that for people who haven't been under fire it would be very difficult, especially in urban environment where sound bounces off walls and down streets, to establish the exact shooting positions.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: So you made an independent determination?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And how were you able to determine the ammunition and weapons type when no ammunition was found? Can you give the Chamber an example?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: The factors that I used are the distance. I believe that over 300 metres, the standard ammunition that was used in the conflict which is the 7.62 times 39, which is the round that is used in the AK-47 series of rifles, is inaccurate for ranges over 300 metres. So that would be -- I could -- it's the same if -- I would eliminate ammunition that I thought was very unlikely to have been used. It also depends on the kind of wounds that were sustained. If you would have 12.7 millimetres or a large calibre bullet that would hit a child, the child would have sustained far bigger wounds than some of the cases.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: I'd like to -- well, just referencing your last -- the last part of your answer. Can you, for example, comment in regards to incident F1, the shooting of Anisa Pita, and I'm just referring to the last part of your answer where you said if you would have a 12.7 millimetre or larger calibre bullet that would hit a child, the child would have sustained far bigger wounds.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Yes. The distance that I think the shooter has fired from in case F1, it's over 900 metres, so that would eliminate small calibre of -- short range ammunition like the AK-47 ammunition. If the child would have been hit, she was three years at the -- at that time, then her leg wouldn't have been bigger than my wrist, and she was wounded in her right leg by a 12.7 millimetre bullet, she probably wouldn't have her leg anymore. So that's -- it's almost impossible then for her leg to have been like this. Is she still -- she's still alive. Her leg is still on, so I believe that the 12.7 millimetre bullet wouldn't -- wasn't used in this instance.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: I would like to turn now to the -- to Incident F11, which is the 8 October 1994 injuring of passengers on a tram.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: For Your Honours' and counsel's information, examination of this incident begins in the hard copy on the page marked 39 of 84 and continues onto page 49. In e-court it begins on page 40 of the English and page 49 of the B/C/S, although I'm not asking that it be shown on the monitor at this time.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Now, did you receive, captain, conflicting information about the location of the tram in that F11 incident when it was fired upon?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And can I please have on the monitor 65 ter 10047. And this is the translation of a French language report of the investigation into the 8 October 1994 incident, F11. And if we could turn, please, to page 6 in the English, which is page 5 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Can you explain, captain, generally the conflicting information about the location of the tram that you received?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Yes, I can. The victim mentions an S-curve in the tracks of the tram. That S-curves -- S-curve is right in front of the Holiday Inn hotel. But if I look at the map that the UNPROFOR report has attached, that position is S2 while in the UNPROFOR report they mention spot number 2 which is one intersection to the east. So they mention in the report an incident that took place in front of the Holiday Inn hotel, but then later on they refer to S1 which is an intersection east of that location.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: So let me refer back to the document that's -- that's on the screen, 65 ter 10047. This is a report by a French -- by members of the French Battalion who were on the scene at F11 and contains their conclusions about the incident and location and origin of fire; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And page -- pages 5 through 7 of this report in the English and B/C/S gives a chronology of events. And on the page that we were looking at, which was page 6 in the English and page 5 of the B/C/S, there appears to be a key to the map identifying certain spots; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Now, if we could please bring up on the monitor the French version of the document which is uploaded as the original in e-court and turn to pages -- we can start with page 4. Sorry, we can start -- if we can just move to page 4, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And, sir, I'll continue as it comes up. It's just come up. But in the original French version of the document at pages 4, 5, and 6, there is a map. Is that the map to which the -- the key that we referred to in the other versions pertains?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And did you use this map and the conclusions in this report in your analysis of F11?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: I -- I used this map and I took into account the conclusions in this report.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Okay. And so would -- does this -- does this map assist in understanding the analysis of F11 in your report and the diagrams that you've drawn in your report?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: I believe it does.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender this document, 65 ter 10047 at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 10047 becomes Exhibit P670, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P670 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if we could again please see 65 ter 28541 on the monitor, which is the report, and turn to page 49 in e-court. Again, this can be broadcast. It's page 61 in the B/C/S in e-court, and it is page 48 of 84 in the hard copy.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Now, captain, can you please explain using this -- the diagram in your report the conclusions you drew regarding the origin of fire for each location that you -- each location of the incident occurrence that you examined and - sorry - and explain this diagram to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: The diagram is a cutout of some satellite imaginary, which -- on which I have imposed the markings of the map that we were just shown. The S0 to S3 are the spots mentioned in the French report and in black above the vehicles that were -- the UNPROFOR vehicles that were present at that location. Then the Metalka is -- the name Metalka is a name given to an angled building south of -- in -- in the same line as the Holiday Inn hotel in the S-curve, and the yellow area shows the -- the firing zone that would be able -- that would have been if the shooter would have been in the Metalka building. The Jewish cemetery with houses 9 to 14, those are the houses mentioned in the French report, and the yellow area would be the firing zone from that area to spot 1. I believe that S spot 2 is the location where the tram was hit initially, but I also believe that -- since there's also a video footage of shooting at spot 1 that spot 1 was also under fire. So I believe that the differences in my findings and the UNPROFOR findings come from the fact that there was a prolonged incidents and that shooting took place from both locations, so the Metalka as well as the Jewish cemetery.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And so the -- just to follow up on that, the FrenchBat conclusion was that the shooting was from the Jewish cemetery. Is that what this reflects?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And that -- that the origin of fire was from Metalka. Is that your conclusion?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: The conclusion where the tram was hit, that is my conclusion. From the Metalka building.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And do those two -- those two different conclusions, do those reflect two different beliefs about where the location of the tram was, either at spot 1 or spot 2?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: The exact location of the tram is not the same in -- in most of the reports. However, the witness who was in the tram and the victims, they described the location at the S-curve, as well as the -- the initial lines -- the first lines of the UN report, and I do believe that the tram was at that location when it was hit.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: But since the tram was moving it would also automatically move aware from that spot towards spot 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And that location that you've just described is reflected by S2; is that correct? The location by the Holiday Inn.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Now, did you, despite your conclusion that -- that the tram was likely located closer to S2, did you analyse the origin of fire if the spot -- if the tram was located at S1 where the FrenchBat report has it located?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Well, if the tram had been located at S1, then the FrenchBat report would be accurate in identifying houses 9 to 14 as the origin of fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: So if -- if it was at S1, you would agree with their conclusion, but you find your analysis leads you to the opinion that it was located at S2 with an origin of fire at the Metalka building.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I, at this point in time, put an additional question for my better understanding. You mentioned the possibility that the tram was moving while it was shot at. Was it moving from S1 to S2 or the other way around in your view?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The tram line, the tracks that the tram was on, those are the -- it's a track that is going from west to east, so towards the city centre. That's also the direction that is described in the witness reports and the UN report, so the tram was moving from west to east and that would be from S2 to S1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: I would like to turn now, please, to incident -- the incident labelled F12 which is the 18 November 1994 shooting of Mrs. Sokolovic and the killing of her son, Nermin. For everyone's information, in the hard copy of the report the analysis begins at page 50. In e-court it begins on page 51 in the English and page 63 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Now, did you receive information -- I'm sorry. Did you receive differing information for the exact location of these victims when they were shot?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And I -- I'll ask Ms. Stewart to please play 65 ter 22452J, which is a segment of a video of investigator Barry Hogan with Ms. Sokolovic, and I'll ask if you could play it, please, from 40 seconds, to one minute and two seconds. And, Your Honours, with this witness I'm not going to rely on the audio and so it does not need to be played twice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we'll not listen, but, rather, look.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Sorry, it actually occurs to me that we could -- we don't have to play the entire segment. I just said we can stop it right there, since we're just looking at it. And I've just stopped it at 48.5.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Captain, does the location we see in the video that has just been played correspond with the GPS co-ordinates that you list in your report with regard to this F12 incident?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Okay. And did you consider that location on the street as a possible location of the -- of the shooting, where it occurred?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Did location -- this location would be a possibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Now, I'll ask Your Honours that -- that 22452J be marked for identification. The Prosecution will seek to tender it at a later time through another witness when the audio portions will also be relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar informs me that she hasn't received any video.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Sorry, I apologise. That we do have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the usher assist --

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: We do have it here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the usher assist in... Madam Registrar, the number to be assigned to a video of which we only saw a still at 48.5 seconds would receive number ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Video 22452J receives number P671, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Now, I will also -- I'll now ask Ms. Stewart to play the first 13 seconds of what is already in evidence as P136, and I would just note that on -- this is a duplicate of what's listed on the exhibit list for this witness as 65 ter 22352.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But there's no need to uses the duplicate. We just show the --

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Yes. Just P136.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's look at the portion played.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Yes. And that video was just stopped at 20.9 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: The location in which we saw the -- the boy on the ground in the zebra crossing in that video, did you also consider that as a possible location of where the actual incident occurred in F11 when assessing the origin of fire?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I believe that this location on the zebra crossing is the exact location where that boy was shot.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Now, if we, again, could look at 65 ter 28541, which is the report on the monitor, in e-court at page 52 of the English and 64 of the B/C/S, and this can be broadcast outside of the courtroom. And it's on page 51 of the hard copy. Now, is the range of distance between -- between and including the two different locations we have just seen in these two videos reflected in your analysis and diagrams on page 51?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: I haven't listed the location that is visible in the video of the -- of the witness interview, so the location of the victim is the -- is -- the only one that I have used in this diagram is the one that was visible from the video footage of the boy on the zebra crossing.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And when you say this diagram, can you tell us -- there are two on the page. Can you just tell us which you're referring to? Or both.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: It would be the close-up of the incident site that's -- on the layout of the incident site. There it's slightly more to the west.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: So the layout -- the -- the first diagram, titled "Layout of the Incident Site," is the blue circle marking the location of the victim is slightly more toward where the GPS co-ordinates that you considered based on the mother's interview with Barry Hogan; is that right? Does that accurately state that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: The GPS co-ordinates were given to me by the OTP and are the same as the location where the investigator had the interview. So that would -- that is correct. And that circle is more that position.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us, did you analyse the entire range from where the interview took place to where we see the boy laying in the street for the origin of fire and direction of fire?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I believe that on either one of -- either of the locations the boy would have been visible from someone in the Metalka building, and the more he would move -- walk towards the road, so towards the east, the more he would be visible.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: So is -- are -- do the differing locations change your opinion in this incident?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: No, they do not.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's been pointed out to me that this might be time to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is the appropriate time to have a break. Could the witness be escorted out of the courtroom first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break, and we resume at 10 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, Mr. Lukic, the Chamber was informed that Mr. Mladic doesn't feel well and that he would prefer to return to the UNDU and lie down; but also that he wants to waive his right to be present at trial. Could we seek confirmation from Mr. Mladic. Mr. Mladic, is that your position at this moment, that you would prefer to return to the UNDU and that you waive your right to be present in court at this moment?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, I feel very poorly in terms of my health. I need hospital treatment. I have grown weaker and weaker in the last 10 to 15 days. I have lost my appetite. I should go to hospital as soon as possible and receive treatment. This is unbearable for me. I'd sooner go there and be bedridden and die there than stay here listening to foolishness, to NATO propaganda.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I didn't invite you to comment on the testimony of the witness. Have you reported your not being well to the medical service of the United Nations Detention Unit over the last ten days? Mr. Mladic, did you report it over the last ten days? Mr. Lukic, do you have any information about it being reported?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yesterday I was in touch with Dr. Falke and with the lady doctor, the English woman, who asks for me to sign statements about how I feel. I told them that I urgently needed to go to hospital to undergo a thorough check, a medical check. I have lost my appetite, and in the last ten days I spent most of my time in bed. And if this isn't enough...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well whether that is not enough or not, we would wait for any medical report which we did not receive. Now my next question is you had said you prefer to go back to the UNDU, and as I understand now, you would urge the doctors to send you to hospital. The next question is when you leave this courtroom, do you want us to -- do you waive your right to be present so that we can continue, or would you say, No, I insist on being present during the remainder of the testimony of this witness, to start with? What is your position? If you want to consult with counsel, you have an opportunity to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Orie, rather than talk extensively about it, I will try and remain seated here in this chair even if I should die here. Your procedure here will not help me. I will not waive my right to defend myself until the very last moment to defend myself from NATO lies and this so-called court of yours. You are no court of law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are a corrupt group --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, Mr. Mladic should further remain silent. I do understand from his last answer that he would prefer to stay in this courtroom. We'll then proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you give me one more minute, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll continue with Mr. Mladic in the courtroom for now, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Meanwhile, Ms. Hochhauser, revisiting the matter of the confidential exhibits and the redacted public version, the public version should be filed, not be tendered. That is the practice in this Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: As we're waiting for the witness to be brought in, can we -- can I ask for to 28609 to be placed on the monitor. That will be the next exhibit that we start with. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you may proceed, Ms. Hochhauser.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to turn now briefly to the scheduled -- the scheduled occurrence F3, which is the 11 July 1993 shooting of Munira Zametica on the banks of the Dobrinja river.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And in front of you on the monitor should be -- is -- is, 65 ter 28609. And this is an information report from Sadija Sahinovic, dated 14 September 2001. And I draw your attention to where it states that: "On the day that Zametica was killed, the water level was lower than today. It was so low that Munira had to be further out toward the middle than it is possible to mark on the bank today." Does the analysis of F3 in your report, which for everybody's information begins at page 17 in the hard copy of the report, does your analysis as contained in the report account for this information; and, if so, how does it affect your opinion?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: It does affect the report. The lower the water level, the more you are in a kind of a tunnel formed by the banks of the canal and the more precise the direction is where the shooter must have been, and so I took into account the water level and I lowered myself down to the water level, which was also low at the time that I visited that location. It was approximately knee level, the water of -- the depth of the water, and checked from there from the banks at eye height that -- to see if -- to try to determine the point of origin.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And does the difference in the water level as described here change your conclusion as to the point of origin?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: No, it doesn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I put an additional question. What we see now on the screen is on the day that Zametica was killed, the water level was lower than today. Now do you have any idea about how much lower it was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the water level --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I mean, 1 centimetre, 10 centimetres?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no idea, Your Honour, how low the level would have been. But if you had to walk out to it, almost to the middle of the canal -- the canal is not that wide, it's only a few metres wide from bank -- from top of the bank to the other bank, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say if.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But you have got no idea about the quantity of --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't know exactly what the depth at the time was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Not at the time of the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- incident. Not at the time of this report which we see on the screen where it says the water level was lower than today. How much lower, you have no idea?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Though -- I know it was lower because when I visited the water level was about knee depth and with the markings on the side of the water you can see the algae, you can see that the markings on the side of the canal, what the water levels are like, and there were -- was a lot of markings above the water level that -- when I visited it. So it can't have been much lower because it was already below knee depth when I visited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But that is on an assumption --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- that these higher levels would have been reached at any time at all, which is just an assumption.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I've seen on a lot of these scales untouched levels for very long time. So you don't have any knowledge about the level at the time. You don't have any knowledge about the difference of level on the day this report was made on the 8th of October, 2001. Neither do you have any specific knowledge about the water level when you visited the place, apart from that in your guess, estimate, it was relatively low.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Which -- would you agree with me that this makes it very difficult to make any accurate calculations which whether or not and to what extent it would have affected your findings.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree, Your Honour, because the -- it's not a natural canal. It's man-made, it's concrete banks, and the banks themselves, even if they are at the top of the concrete, it's already -- there's an earth bank all the way to the top, and even if you're already at the level of the concrete bank, then that is already forms a -- already forms a natural tunnel in -- no. Let's see. What was it? In general east or west direction. So, yes, there is -- it's difficult to exactly determine how deep the water was at the time, but the banks themselves, they still form a natural tunnel which would -- it only makes it more accurate to know what the -- what the level was exactly at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because that would be -- would determine most likely the position of the victim.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Who approached the water to take water out of the canal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Please proceed, Ms. Hochhauser.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Perhaps if we look at Exhibit P3, which is the Sarajevo map book. That's page 9 in the hard copy. I'm just, sorry, looking for the e-court page. Sorry. As I'm looking for the e-court page, I'll just continue to ask a question.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Which is: Captain, your assessment of the line of sight for that F3 incident from the building that you determined as the origin of fire, how does it -- how does the line of sight change depending on how far you are up the bank?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: It doesn't change. It doesn't matter how far you were up or down the bank, you would still be visible, in clear view of that building.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Thank you. And it's on page 13 in e-court, is the map I was looking for.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Thank you, Janet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one additional question in this respect. Couldn't you climb up the bank that much that you'd be covered by the bridge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only if you would be -- if only you would be able to get the bridge between you and the -- and the building. But if you would be under the bridge, you would still be silhouetted in the shadows.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Which means that your previous answer that it doesn't matter is incorrect. If you climb high enough to be behind the bridge on the bank, although that most likely could not be the water level, because the level of the water would then be higher than the bridge allows it to be. But the higher you climb, the more there is a chance that you will be covered by the bridge, that the line of sight would be interrupted by the bridge itself.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You would have to climb really high because it's only a very small bridge which doesn't have any reinforcements on either side. It's just a -- well, like a big slab of concrete. But if there were -- there were people hiding under the bridge, so she might -- if she would be high enough, the shooter would have to shoot through other people to -- to hit the target.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I have not -- I don't know whether that's material which was given to you. But people said, Don't go that down because you might be hit by a sniper, whereas if you stayed a bit higher up the bank that people felt safe and not being sniped at.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the only explanation that I -- I might have is that at that time I can't imagine that people were cutting the grass on the banks of the river a lot because it was in a -- it was in a dangerous area, so the grass might have been higher for people to hide in. They would still be vulnerable to fire -- to shooting but less visible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Through the grass.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Through the grass, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any information about the -- I mean, if grass, in my experience, is usually up to, well, anything between 5 and 25 centimetres, whereas persons sitting in the grass usually are at least half a metre if not more up. So I'm slightly surprised by your explanation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't mean grass exactly but just -- trying to find the English word for it. Just undergrowth in general, neglected -- just wild flowers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whatever kind of bush --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nettles, they grow a lot higher than regular grass. So -- if the -- but it's again an "if." If the banks weren't cared for for a longer time, then you might have vegetation that would reach up to a metre, approximately [Overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- at the most. It's a guess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's speculation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Hochhauser.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I had put the -- the photograph on the monitor from the map book at page 13.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: I don't want to belabour the point, but if that assists at all in -- in pointing out on the -- on that image where it was approximately that you were standing when you went and where it was that the GPS co-ordinates that were given to you indicated in terms of height up on the bank?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: The photo itself, it helps. The GPS co-ordinates, it's always -- there's always an inaccuracy, that's why the combination of the GPS location and the location that was pointed out by the investigator and therefore the witnesses, so the victims, the water level was lower when I visited because here it's -- it's pretty high. But it's -- that's the same building that I determined to be the point of origin. Although according to the witness statements, the building wasn't finished at that time. It was more only the structure itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And is it -- can you give us a description on this image that we're looking at of where you would have been standing in reliance on the GPS co-ordinates that were given to you by the investigator?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: If I would be down at the -- describe the location that I took the photograph from, it would be up to ankle level in the water. So it would be on the -- if I look at this photo, at the left side of the water, and then with my feet in the water.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Okay. Captain, in you're Appendix A to the report, you list weapons and ammunition used by the VRS along with their effective ranges, and if we could put, please, 65 ter 28500 on the monitor. And that is the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade, document number 3-1335/2, information on sniper rifles, silencers, passive and infrared equipment, dated 29 October 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And for everybody's information, Appendix A begins at 86 in e-court and is the first page is directly following -- unnumbered, directly following page 84 in the hard copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we would object to the use of this document in so far as the same was not identified in the expert report prepared by this witness and was not discussed in any detail in the findings of the expert report, so we believe that this is a direct violation of Rule 94 bis, and a very serious one at that. We have brought this objection to the attention of Your Honours in our response to the Rule 94 bis submission of the Prosecution, and this is one of the 31 documents that were disclosed to us recently which are of the nature that they were not identified in the expert report nor was the subject matter of the same discussed in the expert report, and we believe for an expert witness that all findings, all conclusions are supposed to be in the expert report if Rule 94 bis is to have any significance or meaning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Hochhauser.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Your Honours, the witness was asked to -- asked for his comment on this document during a subsequent proofing and those comments were disclosed to the Defence, an initial comment on the proofing note of 27/28 November 2012. It can be found in point 7K, and, again, a comment in -- on 7 January 2013 of just one sentence at point 4. The -- I would just add to that, while the document is not one that the witness relied on in coming to his conclusion, I think that the comments that were provided show that it substantiates and supports his conclusions and provides illustrative information to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In what way does it support the conclusions and -- I mean, if the witness doesn't use it in support of his conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Well, Judge, there is an appendix in his report that lists weapons and calibre typings along with their maximum effective range. In fact, I think that inclusion of some of this information was a point raised by the Defence in their objection, that he doesn't have the expertise to talk about this, and this report, just for an example, lists weapons that -- it's -- it's an SRK document that would support what is written in his report about what weaponry was available to the SRK at that time and his -- his -- what he says about their maximum effective ranges and abilities, and I think that is material information that this witness is qualified to comment on. His comment has been provided to the Defence, and I think it would -- it is information that could assist the Chamber in its analysis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, if I understand the Prosecution well, they say, well, to the extent, and perhaps they would expect that you would challenge the information provided in appendix A, that this document could be relevant to assess the merits of such a challenge.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, the challenge was to the source of the witness's findings and conclusions. I want to know what he looked at to make these conclusions. They cannot use a document he has not looked at to say this is where he got the information from, so it's actually going at the issue from the wrong side, from the back end instead of the front end. The comments of the witness as to this document from 7 January, 2013, are merely that the M48 7.9 rifle, listed at number 1, is the most accurate long-distance rifle. There is no additional information as to how this relates to the findings in his -- in his appendix and his conclusion; and, again, the objection was where did this information come from so as to see whether his methodology was an appropriate one for an expert witness. And I think that saying, Well, look, we now have a document that he didn't look at does not address that objection, which was the thrust of our objection.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: If I just might, because I gave an example of what the witness could comment on this from this document, but I would also say that there is an additional comment from the -- on that document in the November proofing note, which -- in which the witness stated that it demonstrates that the listed sniper rifles, scopes, and silencers were issued to sharpshooters and shooters without specialised training, again something that is directly related to topics in his report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Hochhauser, we should clearly distinguish between the sources used by the witness when preparing and drafting his report and any other evidentiary material which the witness may have seen at a later stage and may be able to comment on. So Mr. Ivetic's objections are dealt with in the following way. We should clearly find out what is the source of what the witnesses wrote. For example, in Appendix A about these -- the availability of this weaponry for the VRS at the time, and then once we've done that, we may revisit the use of the document you asked to be brought to the attention the witness. But that's the proper order of dealing with the matter. And then, Mr. Ivetic, once we have followed this procedure we will, at that point in time, then further discuss the appropriateness of using the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Captain, turning to Appendix A, can you tell us, please, what the source of that information is?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: The source of the information in Appendix A is most of all the Jane's Infantry Weapons which is the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Van der Weijden, again I have to intervene. There are distinct issues there. I think that perhaps not the most important one is what is the calibre rate of fire, et cetera, which is all technical stuff. The first and most important question is: What is the source of knowledge of this witness that these weapons were used by the VRS. That's the first question. Could you please answer that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. The Jane's Infantry Weapons 2000/2001, it lists the weapons produced in countries and its use by the main armies, so it specifies that the -- that these weapons were used in Yugoslavia during that time. It doesn't describe -- it doesn't mention by which units they were used. I have been in Yugoslavia during UNPROFOR times myself and I have driven through several VRS check-points and I have witnessed those weapons in the hands of combatants by myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: All of them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: All of them. So you say it is not specified as to be used by the VRS in your written sources but by personal observation you saw all of these weapons in the hands of VRS soldiers during your tenure in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, because that's -- that's why I limited it to those weapons while there are other possibilities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That is an answer to the -- yes, Judge Fluegge may have one more question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just in relation to the record, can you please repeat the title of this document you mentioned in page 38, line 21. It's not recorded properly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's "Jane's Infantry Weapons, 2000/2001."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ivetic, would you also need further sources of information about the calibre maximal effective range or? I mean, that seems to be very technical, if -- would you insist Ms. Hochhauser to first explore that?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: She can do her direct the way she wants, Your Honours. I might raise some matters in cross. It's a matter for Your Honours to consider the totality of the evidence and to determine the -- whether the reports meets the specifications to be an expert report and what weight to be given to it itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we should ask the witness what is the source of the column dealing with the calibre and the maximum effective range.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The calibre and the rate of fire described in the same source, so in Jane's Infantry Weapons, as well as the maximum effective range. The text that I've added is my own experience. I fired most of the -- of these weapons myself, and I've -- in a version or other, but I've fired most of those calibres. So it's from personal experience that I added some of the text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those answers. One second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, your objection against the use of the document still stands or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I guess it will now depend on what questions are asked from the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's then first hear the questions. Ms. Hochhauser, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Captain, if I could just ask one follow-up about the source that you cited, Jane's Infantry Weapons. Is that -- is that a document that's commonly used or source that's commonly used in your field of small armaments?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: The Jane's Infantry Weapons is a renowned source for information in this field.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And do you keep up on advancements in the field of infantry weapons and specifically small arms?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Yes. Constantly.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And is this a -- was this -- sorry, back in the time of the conflict and continued to be a source that is used commonly in the field -- in your field and relied upon?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: So turning to the document that is on the screen, 28500, I'd like to draw your attention to the list of weapons there at 1 through 9 and ask you whether there are weapons that appear on that list with a range of 800 metres -- well, withdrawn. I'll actually rephrase the question. Are those weapons listed at 1 through 9 consistent with what we see listed in your report at Appendix A?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: The -- there would be -- the only deviation would the M48 because the M48 is not listed on the first page. It's only listed on the fourth page of the appendix because at the time of the conflict the M48 was already out of the regular inventory. So it was -- they were in older stocks but available.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Okay. And the M48 -- sorry. Excuse me, I'll begin the question again. Again, drawing your attention to that list, are there weapons on that list with a range of 800 metres or greater?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Yes, there are. I do see a mistake. It's not in the translation because the original also states -- for number 3 it mentions the M48, 7.62 machine-gun, but that most likely would be the M84, 7.62 machine-gun because there was no M48 machine-gun in that conflict.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And are you referring to the English translation on the document at point 3?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Both. Because I see in the original document that number 3 also states M48.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Now -- I'm sorry, did someone -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: I tried to -- sorry. For number 2 and number 6, I would not be able to determine what kind of rifles they were. If they were of the calibre 7.62 times 39, then they would be inadequate for ranges over 300 metres.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And the ones that are listed as sniper rifles are those specialised equipment?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Sniper rifles per definition is specialised equipment.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Now I'd like to also draw your attention --

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And Your Honours, I would move on still within this document to a different topic within it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: So I'd like to draw your attention to the sentences below that list which begins: "As we don't have a special sniper unit, we have issued the sniper rifles" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. To draw our attention to certain matters is argument rather than eliciting testimony. If the document is in evidence --

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry, Judge. I was going to call the witness's attention to it and ask him for comment, but I was drawing the Chamber's attention to the fact that I was moving off of the -- the Appendix A-related information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If the witness can tell us anything about what remains, then please -- you have drawn his attention to the two lines following the list of weaponry, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Correct. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If the witness has read that, you may ask questions about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Beginning with "As we don't have a special sniper unit" and ending with "in the subordinated units," if you could look at that.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: I have read it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And I would like to ask for your comment on that portion of the document given your -- what your report addresses about the equipment and training for snipers.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Well, here they state they don't have a special sniper unit. That would indicate they don't have people within the unit that have sniper training and that they have issued those weapons to combatants in the subordinated units. That's probably -- they probably issued the rifles to the most experienced riflemen for them to use it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, at this time I would tender that document 28500?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Before doing so could I ask a few questions, a more thorough analysis of these two lines. As we don't have a special sniper unit, it seems that you conclude from that, that in other units, perhaps not special sniper units, there were no trained snipers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I conclude that in this unit they didn't have snipers because usually it's an assumption, of course, snipers are combined into a -- into teams, so that's why I concluded that they issued the sniper rifles to the most experienced marksmen instead of snipers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But the most experienced marksmen could have had specific sniper training.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He could have. He could also be an experienced hunter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we just don't know. You tendered the document. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection based on the discussions that the witness has had with the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 28500 becomes Exhibit P672, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P672 is admitted into evidence. You may proceed, Ms. Hochhauser.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Now, I would like to turn to document 1550 on the monitor. And, again, this is a document that was commented on in -- in -- in proofings, and the witness provides comment on but was not relied upon by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It is on their list, Your Honours, as one of the 31 documents that was the subject of our objection in the response to the 94 bis submission of the Prosecution and would be for the same reason that, again, this is -- does not appear to be a document that has been utilised by this witness in the preparation of his report, and I will leave any further objections based upon questions that are raised, if, in fact, they are ones that are not within the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll first listen to the questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And that is number 15550. Sorry, if I miss -- I left out of a 5, I believe. And as that's going up on the monitor, it's the VRS Main Staff situation report, dated 5 November 1995. I'm not sure if anybody else is seeing the document. I'm not. Ah --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I had already on my second screen but now we have it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And, captain, are you seeing this document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: I'm seeing it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And if we could -- if you could just take a look at the whole document and I'll also specifically draw your attention to paragraph on -- if we could turn to page 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it's page 2 in the English but remains page 1 in the B/C/S. Titled: "Combat Readiness Situation." And in your report, you discuss how snipers are generally organised and deployed from your knowledge and experience. And in light of that experience, can you give us your comment on that paragraph that I've drawn your attention to in 65 ter 15550?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
